items.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Common-law courts have always preferred bright-line rules to flexible standards.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Modern federal procedure has eliminated all procedural barriers facing pro se litigants.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The drafters of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure rejected the influence of the common-law tradition.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Twombly and Iqbal returned the federal courts to nineteenth-century pleading standards.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The shift from rigid pleading to notice pleading reflected a deliberate trade of doctrinal predictability for procedural access.

items.explanation: The passage's central thesis is that the move to notice pleading was a *trade-off*: the drafters knowingly sacrificed some predictability to widen the courthouse door. E captures both halves. A overstates ('always'). B is contradicted by the closing paragraph. C is too strong — the passage says drafters were *informed by* the tradition, not that they rejected it. D confuses the post-Iqbal tightening with a full reversion.

items.stem: The author's attitude toward Twombly and Iqbal is best described as one of…

choices.label: A
choices.text: uncritical endorsement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: open hostility.

choices.label: C
choices.text: qualified concern.

choices.label: D
choices.text: indifference.

choices.label: E
choices.text: scholarly bewilderment.

items.explanation: The author concedes that the cases addressed real problems (mass-tort fishing expeditions) but worries they 'risk reintroducing the very access barrier the 1938 drafters set out to dismantle.' That hedged worry is qualified concern (C), not endorsement, hostility, indifference, or bewilderment.

items.stem: According to the passage, the original Federal Rules of Civil Procedure took effect in…
items.explanation: Detail question. The passage states that 'the original Federal Rules of Civil Procedure … took effect in 1938.' 1957 is the year of Conley v. Gibson; the other dates appear nowhere as the adoption year.

items.stem: The author mentions the Field Code of 1848 primarily in order to…

choices.label: A
choices.text: argue that fact pleading was superior to the notice pleading that followed it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate an early reform effort that solved some problems but introduced new ones.

choices.label: C
choices.text: show that New York courts led all other jurisdictions in procedural innovation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: demonstrate that the writ system was never genuinely abandoned.

choices.label: E
choices.text: establish that procedural reform inevitably fails.

items.explanation: The Field Code is introduced as a 'partial remedy' to the writ system, but the next paragraph explains that 'fact pleading … generated its own pathologies.' B captures that role — an early reform that helped yet created new problems. A and E overstate the point; C and D assert claims the passage never makes.

items.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred from the passage that defenders of Twombly and Iqbal believe that…

choices.label: A
choices.text: notice pleading should be abolished entirely.

choices.label: B
choices.text: pro se litigants rarely file meritorious claims.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Conley v. Gibson was wrongly decided from the outset.

choices.label: D
choices.text: changes in litigation since 1938 justify a more demanding pleading standard.

choices.label: E
choices.text: the Field Code offered a better model than the Federal Rules.

items.explanation: Defenders 'note that mass-tort and antitrust complaints had created discovery abuses the 1938 drafters could not have foreseen' — i.e., new litigation conditions warrant a tougher standard, which is D. A, B, C, and E go well beyond anything the defenders are said to claim.

items.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Privity of contract was an indefensible doctrine that nineteenth-century courts should have abandoned far sooner than they did.

choices.label: B
choices.text: American products-liability law moved from a privity bar through negligence to strict liability, yet strict liability retains substantial elements of negligence reasoning.

choices.label: C
choices.text: MacPherson v. Buick eliminated the requirement that an injured consumer prove a manufacturer's negligence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Restatement (Second) of Torts settled the long-running dispute over the proper basis of manufacturer liability.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Justice Traynor's concurrence in Escola was the most influential single opinion in the history of American tort law.

items.explanation: The passage traces an arc — privity bar, then negligence after MacPherson, then strict liability — and closes by stressing that strict liability still 'sits uneasily' with negligence reasoning. B captures both the arc and that tension. A states an evaluative claim the author never makes. C is false: the passage says MacPherson 'did not abolish the need to prove fault.' D is contradicted by the final paragraph, which says the question is still 'debatable.' E overstates a detail and is not the passage's overall point.

items.stem: According to the passage, the doctrine of privity of contract was crystallized in which one of the following cases?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Winterbottom v. Wright.

choices.label: B
choices.text: MacPherson v. Buick Motor Co.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Escola v. Coca-Cola Bottling Co.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Greenman v. Yuba Power Products.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Conley v. Gibson.

items.explanation: Detail question. The first paragraph states that privity of contract was 'crystallized in the English case Winterbottom v. Wright (1842).' MacPherson (B) cracked the privity rule; Escola (C) and Greenman (D) belong to the strict-liability story; Conley v. Gibson (E) is a civil-procedure case that does not appear in this passage at all.

items.stem: The author refers to Justice Traynor's concurrence in Escola primarily in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: demonstrate that strict liability had already become the governing rule by 1944.

choices.label: B
choices.text: identify an early judicial argument for strict liability that courts would adopt only later.

choices.label: C
choices.text: criticize the Escola majority for reasoning that was internally inconsistent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: show that Cardozo's approach in MacPherson had been formally overruled.

choices.label: E
choices.text: establish that risk distribution is an inadequate justification for liability.

items.explanation: The passage presents the 1944 concurrence as urging a change that 'prevailed a generation later' in Greenman (1963) and §402A (1965) — i.e., an early argument adopted only afterward, which is B. A misreads the timeline (it was a concurrence, not the governing rule). C and D describe moves the author never makes. E states a critique the author raises only as one side of a 'debatable' question, not the reason for citing Traynor.

items.stem: The author's attitude toward describing modern products-liability law as 'strict' is best characterized as one of

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic agreement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: measured skepticism.

choices.label: C
choices.text: outright rejection of strict liability as a concept.

choices.label: D
choices.text: indifference to how the doctrine is labeled.

choices.label: E
choices.text: nostalgia for the privity requirement.

items.explanation: In the final paragraph the author concedes strict liability's risk-distribution rationale but warns that the 'strict-liability label can obscure how much negligence reasoning survives within it' — a hedged, doubting stance toward the label, i.e., measured skepticism (B). A is too positive. C overstates: the author questions the label, not the doctrine's existence. D is wrong because the author plainly cares about the label's accuracy. E finds no support; the author calls privity a remedyless 'price' borne by consumers.

items.stem: According to the passage, the appellate court in People v. Collins reversed the conviction on which one of the following grounds?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The underlying trait frequencies were unproven, and they were multiplied together as if each trait were independent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The one-in-twelve-million figure was too small to support any inference of guilt.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Statistical evidence is categorically inadmissible in criminal trials.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The eyewitnesses' descriptions of the couple conflicted with one another.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The prosecution introduced no physical evidence linking the couple to the crime.

items.explanation: Paragraph 2 states that the court reversed because the individual frequencies 'were never established by evidence' and that multiplying them 'assumed, without proof, that each trait was statistically independent.' A restates exactly that ground. B misreads the objection — the court faulted the figure's foundation, not its size, and the passage never says a small probability cannot support an inference. C overstates: the paragraph on DNA shows statistics are not categorically barred. D and E describe facts (conflicting descriptions, missing physical evidence) the passage never mentions.

items.stem: According to the passage, the doctrine of prior appropriation differs from the riparian doctrine in that prior appropriation

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats flowing water as a resource held in common by every landowner the stream touches.

choices.label: B
choices.text: forbids any user from depleting the flow so as to defeat a neighbor's reasonable use.

choices.label: C
choices.text: assigns water rights to whoever first diverted the water to a beneficial use, independent of land ownership.

choices.label: D
choices.text: allocates water through time-limited permits issued by an administrative agency.

choices.label: E
choices.text: guarantees every claimant a proportional share of the water during a shortage.

items.explanation: Paragraph 2 states that prior appropriation 'severed water rights from land ownership entirely and awarded them instead to whoever first diverted the water and put it to a recognized beneficial use.' C restates exactly that. A and B describe the riparian doctrine of paragraph 1 (water 'held in common' and the bar on so depleting the flow as 'to defeat a neighbor's reasonable use'), not appropriation. D describes the regulated-riparian permit regime of paragraph 3, not appropriation. E is contradicted: under appropriation a senior holder 'took a full allotment while junior holders received nothing,' so no proportional share is guaranteed.

items.stem: According to the passage, the Court of King's Bench relied on a legal fiction in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: codify a rule that the legislature had declined to enact

choices.label: B
choices.text: conceal from the public the identity of the judges who governed them

choices.label: C
choices.text: hear cases that would otherwise have fallen outside its authority

choices.label: D
choices.text: relieve overcrowding among the prisoners in its custody

choices.label: E
choices.text: establish that a fictitious trespass was itself an actionable wrong

items.explanation: The first paragraph explains that the King's Bench 'could ordinarily try only prisoners already in its custody, so it invented the supposition' of a fictitious trespass — a pretense that 'quietly extended the court's reach far beyond its original bounds.' (C) captures exactly this jurisdiction-expanding purpose and is correct. (A) fails because the passage says 'no statute authorized the maneuver'; the fiction substituted for legislation rather than codifying any rule the legislature had refused to pass. (B) imports Bentham's later charge of deceit, but the paragraph describes the aim as enlarging authority, not hiding the judges' identities. (D) misreads the 'custody,' which was itself the fiction — the court was not thinning out real prisoners. (E) inverts the device: the trespass was a pretense used to reach the case, not a wrong the court sought to establish as actionable.

items.stem: The author refers to People v. Collins primarily in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: prove that eyewitness identifications are inherently unreliable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate how the appearance of mathematical precision can lend false certainty to an unsupported factual premise.

choices.label: C
choices.text: establish that appellate courts rarely disturb jury verdicts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: endorse the prosecution's method of multiplying trait frequencies.

choices.label: E
choices.text: show that criminal convictions require a higher probability than civil liability.

items.explanation: Paragraph 2 presents Collins 'as a caution against the aura of certainty that a large number can lend to a shaky factual premise' — precisely the role B names. A misidentifies the lesson as being about eyewitness reliability rather than the misuse of probability. C asserts a claim the passage never makes, and Collins was itself a reversal. D reverses the author's stance; both the court and the author criticize the multiplication. E imports the criminal-versus-civil burden contrast, which belongs to the gatecrasher discussion, not to why Collins is cited.

items.stem: According to the passage, proponents of actuarial risk-assessment instruments claim that the instruments do which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Eliminate the need for a judge to review a defendant's case file.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Apply a uniform standard to defendants whose circumstances are alike.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Guarantee that no defendant will be wrongly detained before trial.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Predict rearrest more accurately than any human expert could.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Remove race entirely from bail and sentencing decisions.

items.explanation: The second paragraph credits the instruments with the ability to 'impose a welcome consistency, ensuring that similarly situated defendants are scored by the same yardstick,' which is precisely (B). (A) is never claimed; the case file is mentioned only as part of the older discretionary practice. (C) overstates; nothing in the passage promises a guarantee against wrongful detention. (D) overshoots the modest claim that an instrument can 'flag patterns that an overworked judge... will miss'—that is not a claim of superiority over any human expert. (E) is contradicted by the third paragraph, where the author says the proxies actually track race rather than removing it.

items.stem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Legal fictions are defensible devices whose value depends on their remaining openly recognized as fictions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Legal fictions were indispensable to the early common law but have no place in a modern codified system.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bentham and Fuller reached incompatible conclusions only because they examined different historical periods.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The fiction of corporate personhood shows why courts should abandon metaphorical reasoning altogether.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Judicial lawmaking is illegitimate whenever it proceeds by way of a fiction rather than open declaration.

items.explanation: The fourth paragraph states the thesis: the author 'leans toward Fuller, but with a qualification' — a fiction 'is worth its cost only so long as it remains visible as a fiction,' since a labeled fiction 'invites the very reform Bentham wanted' while a hardened one 'buries a contestable policy choice.' (A) states exactly this and is correct. (B) echoes Bentham's position, which the author rejects, and the author never says fictions lack a modern place. (C) seizes on the detail that Fuller wrote 'a century later,' but the passage never blames their disagreement on differing eras, and this is not the central claim. (D) misuses the corporate-personhood example, which Fuller offers to show fictions can honestly express, not to condemn metaphor. (E) restates Bentham's rejected view that fiction-based lawmaking is inherently illegitimate.

items.stem: The passage suggests that Bentham would most likely have regarded a legal system's continued reliance on fictions as evidence that

choices.label: A
choices.text: the system's judges were unusually inventive

choices.label: B
choices.text: the system had successfully avoided unjust outcomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: the system relied too heavily on its legislature

choices.label: D
choices.text: the system's litigants preferred flexibility to predictability

choices.label: E
choices.text: the system's written law had not yet been adequately reformed

items.explanation: Paragraph two reports Bentham's view that a fiction 'was always a confession of failure — proof that the written law had grown inadequate,' and that a codified system 'would dispense with fictions entirely; their persistence was a symptom of arrested legal development.' Combining these, continued reliance on fictions signals to Bentham that the written law remains unreformed, so (E) is correct. (A) contradicts the text, which says persistence was 'not a sign of judicial ingenuity.' (B) overreads: Bentham condemned fictions and would not treat their survival as proof that injustice had been avoided. (C) reverses his commitments — he favored legislative codification and viewed fictions as a sign of too little legislative reform, not excessive reliance on the legislature. (D) attributes the practice to litigants' tastes, a cause the passage never mentions.

items.stem: The author's attitude toward Bentham's critique of legal fictions is best described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: complete agreement with both its conclusion and its reasoning

choices.label: B
choices.text: dismissal of it as wholly without foundation

choices.label: C
choices.text: neutrality born of an unwillingness to take sides

choices.label: D
choices.text: partial validation of its underlying worry combined with rejection of its diagnosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: admiration for its rhetorical force but indifference to its substance

items.explanation: In the final paragraph the author writes that 'Bentham's alarm, then, is not baseless; it simply misidentifies the culprit,' locating the fault in 'the profession's habit of mistaking a useful metaphor for a discovery' rather than in fictions themselves. That is partial endorsement of the worry plus rejection of the diagnosis, so (D) is correct. (A) is too strong — the author sides with Fuller and rejects Bentham's diagnosis. (B) is refuted directly by 'not baseless.' (C) misreads the author, who plainly 'leans toward Fuller' rather than remaining neutral. (E) is unsupported: the author engages Bentham's substance closely, correcting rather than ignoring it.

items.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Courts should abandon their resistance to statistical evidence, which rests on nothing more than innumeracy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People v. Collins demonstrates that probability calculations have no legitimate role in the courtroom.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The law's wariness toward naked statistics is best understood as a demand for individualized, methodologically transparent proof rather than an aversion to numbers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: DNA profiling has resolved the long-standing debate over the admissibility of statistical evidence.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The civil preponderance standard should be raised above the 0.501 threshold to prevent unjust verdicts.

items.explanation: The thesis emerges across paragraphs 3 and 4: the law's resistance 'defends this demand for particularized evidence' and is 'not a superstition about digits,' and quantified proof 'earns its place when its method is auditable and its inference individualized.' C captures both halves. A inverts the author, who endorses the instinct and calls the discomfort 'not mere innumeracy.' B overreads Collins; the DNA example shows numbers can belong in court. D overstates — DNA illustrates the principle rather than resolving the debate. E seizes on the 0.501 detail and urges a reform the passage never proposes.

items.stem: The discussion of the gatecrasher hypothetical (the rodeo attendees) functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: provide a real case in which a court awarded damages on statistical evidence alone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: demonstrate that the preponderance standard is too lenient for civil cases.

choices.label: C
choices.text: concede that naked statistical evidence is usually sufficient to prove liability.

choices.label: D
choices.text: show that a probability can exceed the applicable burden and still fail for want of individualized evidence.

choices.label: E
choices.text: illustrate the transparent methodology that makes DNA evidence acceptable.

items.explanation: In paragraph 3 the author invokes the 0.501 figure — which 'formally exceeds the civil preponderance standard' — to show that 'what the naked number lacks is individualized proof.' D states that role. A is false twice over: the rodeo case is a hypothetical, not a real case, and no one collects. B misreads the point as a complaint about the standard's leniency rather than about missing particularized evidence. C asserts the reverse of the author's conclusion. E attaches the hypothetical to the DNA methodology discussed later, in paragraph 4.

items.stem: The author's attitude toward the current use of actuarial risk-assessment instruments in bail and sentencing is best described as one of…

choices.label: A
choices.text: unreserved enthusiasm.

choices.label: B
choices.text: bemused detachment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: qualified wariness.

choices.label: D
choices.text: outright condemnation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: complete indifference.

items.explanation: The author concedes 'the case for these tools is not frivolous' yet insists that 'my reservation is narrower but firm'—a hedged, cautionary stance, i.e., qualified wariness (C). (A) is wrong because the reservation is explicit and firm. (B) fails because the author is engaged and takes a clear side rather than standing amused and aloof. (D) is expressly ruled out by the refusal 'to condemn them wholesale.' (E) is impossible given how much concern the author registers about opacity and biased proxies.

items.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The riparian and prior appropriation doctrines are equally unsuited to every jurisdiction, whatever its climate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Wherever water has grown scarce, prior appropriation should displace the older riparian doctrine.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The history of water law shows that no legal rule can allocate a scarce resource fairly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because neither the riparian nor the appropriation doctrine adequately meets modern scarcity, regulated riparianism, despite a genuine cost in predictability, is the better framework.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Administrative permit systems have eliminated the disputes that once arose under the common law of water.

items.explanation: The passage argues that because neither pure doctrine 'serves a modern jurisdiction well,' regulated riparianism is 'the more promising path,' while conceding that 'predictability has genuine value.' D captures both the rejection of the two older rules and the qualified preference for regulation. A misstates the thesis—the author faults the two doctrines for a modern jurisdiction, not 'equally' and everywhere. B backs the wrong winner: the author prefers regulated riparianism, not prior appropriation. C is contradicted, since the author thinks a scarce resource can be allocated well. E overstates—the passage never claims permit systems have 'eliminated' disputes.

items.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A doctrine is described; a competing doctrine is shown to be superior; the two are then merged into one rule.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A traditional doctrine is presented; a rival that arose to remedy its limits is introduced; the author advances a synthesizing approach and defends it against an objection.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A problem is posed; two failed solutions are catalogued; the author concludes that the problem is insoluble.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A reform is proposed; historical precedents for it are surveyed; the reform is then abandoned in favor of an older rule.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two doctrines are compared; empirical evidence is marshaled to test each; a policy recommendation follows from the data.

items.explanation: The passage presents the riparian doctrine (paragraph 1), introduces prior appropriation as the rival that 'arose in answer' to riparianism's failure in arid country (paragraph 2), advances regulated riparianism as a synthesis the author endorses (paragraph 3), and defends it against 'the objection most often pressed' (paragraph 4). B tracks that sequence. A is wrong because the rival appropriation doctrine is never shown to be superior. C is wrong because the author treats the problem as soluble, not 'insoluble.' D inverts the structure—no reform is abandoned for an older rule. E is wrong because no empirical evidence or data is marshaled to test the doctrines.

items.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The reasonable-person standard should be replaced with a test that measures each defendant against his own capacities.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because ordinary morality excuses those who do their best, negligence law is fundamentally unjust to the less capable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Although criticized as unfair to those who cannot meet it, the objective standard is best justified as a pragmatic device for allocating the risks of human variation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Courts have increasingly abandoned the objective standard in favor of individualized inquiries into fault.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The exceptions courts make for children and the suddenly incapacitated show that the objective standard is ultimately incoherent.

items.explanation: The thesis spans the whole arc: the passage presents the objection (para 2), answers it by recasting the standard as a risk-allocation rule (para 3), and argues the exceptions confirm that logic (para 4). C captures both the criticism and the author's pragmatic defense. A recommends replacing the standard, the opposite of the author's endorsement. B states the critics' position as though it were the author's conclusion. D asserts a wholesale abandonment the passage denies, noting only 'limited' carve-outs. E calls the standard 'incoherent,' but the author says the carve-outs 'confirm the allocative logic.'

items.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that Fuller would consider the description of a corporation as a 'person' objectionable only if

choices.label: A
choices.text: the legislature had not expressly authorized it

choices.label: B
choices.text: readers came to treat it as a literal fact rather than a shorthand

choices.label: C
choices.text: it were used to enlarge a court's jurisdiction

choices.label: D
choices.text: it appeared in a criminal proceeding rather than a civil one

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bentham's account of judicial deceit turned out to be correct

items.explanation: Paragraph three says Fuller thought the corporate-'person' fiction 'asserts no falsehood' but warned that a fiction 'can curdle into dogma' when 'later readers may forget the silent "as if" and mistake the metaphor for a fact.' The objection therefore arises only when the shorthand is taken literally, so (B) is correct. (A) states a Benthamite condition — legislative authorization — that Fuller never adopts as his test. (C) borrows the jurisdiction example from paragraph one, which has nothing to do with Fuller's criterion for corporate personhood. (D) invents a civil/criminal distinction the passage never draws. (E) is unsupported: Fuller 'declined to join in the condemnation,' so he does not make his objection depend on Bentham being right.

items.stem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following statements about a legal fiction whose artificiality has been forgotten?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It has achieved the kind of permanence that Bentham thought all sound law should have.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is more likely to prompt legislative reform than a fiction that is openly labeled.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It no longer performs the function that led Fuller to defend fictions in the first place.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It exemplifies the honest expression that Fuller distinguished from deception.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It would be endorsed by the author as among the soundest kind of fiction.

items.explanation: Fuller defended fictions as 'an honest device for saying something new,' one that openly expresses a not-yet-named relationship (paragraph three); the author adds that once a fiction hardens and its artificiality is forgotten, 'it does the opposite' of inviting reform and instead 'buries a contestable policy choice beneath the appearance of settled truth' (paragraph four). Combining the two, a forgotten fiction has stopped doing the transparent, expressive work that justified Fuller's defense, so (C) is correct. (A) misattributes to Bentham a taste for entrenched fictions; he wanted them replaced by open codification, not made permanent. (B) reverses the text — the openly labeled fiction, not the forgotten one, 'invites the very reform Bentham wanted.' (D) describes the honest-expression pole, whereas a forgotten fiction is precisely the case where the 'as if' is lost. (E) contradicts the author, for whom 'the soundest fictions are the ones that announce their own eventual obsolescence,' the opposite of a forgotten one.

items.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage as a whole?

items.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of Passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Third-party litigation funding should be prohibited in federal court until Congress acts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Insurance disclosure rules have proven unworkable and should not be extended to litigation funding.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A narrow rule requiring disclosure of a funder's identity would serve recusal and case management without giving defendants a meaningful tactical advantage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Judges are frequently unaware of conflicts of interest, and this is the most serious problem facing the federal courts.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Defendants who learn that a plaintiff is funded will inevitably litigate against the funder rather than on the merits.

items.explanation: A argues for disclosure and then answers the scope objection by narrowing the rule to identity alone, drawing the insurance analogy to show the line is workable. C carries both halves. A overstates — A never proposes prohibition. B reverses the insurance point: A cites insurance as a *successful* precedent. D inflates a supporting example (recusal) into the passage's thesis and adds a superlative A never uses. E states the critics' prediction as though A endorsed it; A calls it an argument about scope that the narrow rule defuses.

items.stem: In the third paragraph of Passage A, the phrase "an argument about scope, not about principle" is used primarily to indicate that the critics' objection

choices.label: A
choices.text: is dishonest and should be disregarded

choices.label: B
choices.text: identifies a real risk that can be addressed by limiting what must be disclosed rather than by abandoning disclosure

choices.label: C
choices.text: applies with equal force to insurance disclosure

choices.label: D
choices.text: rests on an empirical claim that no study has tested

choices.label: E
choices.text: would be persuasive if the practice of litigation funding were smaller

items.explanation: The sentence before grants the objection 'has force'; the sentences after propose a rule limited to identity and nothing more. So the phrase concedes the risk and relocates it to a question of how much must be disclosed — B. A misreads a concession as a dismissal. C reverses the insurance point: A offers insurance as evidence that a narrow line *works*, not as another victim of the objection. D imports an evidentiary complaint the passage never makes. E introduces a size condition found nowhere in the paragraph.

items.stem: Both passages are committed to which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mandatory disclosure of litigation funders should be adopted in every federal district.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The identity of a litigation funder is more important to a court than the terms of the funding agreement.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Existing rules governing who may bring a claim were drafted without contemplating third-party funding.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Courts currently lack information about litigation funding that bears on how funded cases are handled.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Satellite litigation over funding arrangements is a serious risk of any disclosure regime.

items.explanation: A opens by calling funding 'largely invisible to the courts' and builds its case on the judge who 'cannot see'; B says a court told a funder exists 'proceeds exactly as before' because it cannot tell financing from control — both are committed to an information deficit that matters. D. A is A's position, which B declines to reach. B is A's implicit ranking; B argues the terms are what matter. C is B's historical claim; A never addresses standing rules. E is stated by A as the critics' objection and never raised by B at all — a claim one passage makes is not a claim both are committed to.

items.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes how Passage B's treatment of disclosure differs from Passage A's?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passage B denies that courts lack information about funding, whereas Passage A asserts that they lack it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage B treats disclosure as premature absent a substantive standard, whereas Passage A treats it as independently justified by existing judicial needs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passage B regards disclosure as harmful to plaintiffs, whereas Passage A regards it as harmful only to funders.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage B would require disclosure of the funding agreement's terms, whereas Passage A would require only the funder's identity.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage B considers disclosure a matter for legislatures, whereas Passage A considers it a matter for individual districts.

items.explanation: B's closing sentence is the difference: building the reporting requirement 'before the standard it is meant to serve' leaves courts collecting information they cannot use — disclosure is out of order, not wrong. A grounds disclosure in needs courts already have (recusal, settlement management). B captures the contrast. A misstates B, which agrees courts are uninformed and says the information would not help yet. C invents harms neither passage claims. D is close and wrong: B never proposes a disclosure rule of its own beyond one 'calibrated' to a standard that does not yet exist. E supplies an institutional split neither passage draws.

items.stem: The relationship Passage B describes between a funder with settlement-veto rights and the nominal plaintiff is most analogous to which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A homeowner who hires a contractor to renovate a kitchen and approves each change order before work proceeds.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A bank that lends against a business's receivables and is repaid from them regardless of how the business is run.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A record label that advances a musician recording costs, chooses the producer, must approve any release, and recoups so large a share that the musician profits only on an exceptional hit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A tenant who sublets an apartment to a subtenant while remaining liable to the landlord under the original lease.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An insurer that reimburses a policyholder's loss after the policyholder has settled a claim with a third party.

items.explanation: Abstract B's structure: a financier supplies capital, holds a veto over the decisive event, may replace the agent doing the work, and takes so large a return that the named party gains only in an extreme outcome — control transferred while the name stays on the caption. C matches every element in an unrelated domain. A reverses the control: the homeowner approves, the contractor performs. B is the *passive* end of B's spectrum — repaid regardless of how things are run — which is the arrangement B says is unobjectionable. D transfers possession, not control of a claim, and the tenant keeps liability rather than losing direction. E involves no control over the underlying dispute and is post hoc.

items.stem: The author of Passage B's attitude toward the current debate over litigation funding is most accurately described as

choices.label: A

B. A overshoots: B's concern is doctrinal sequencing, not market growth. C is contradicted by 'there is no doctrine on which it could act'. D ignores the evaluative language throughout. E is contradicted by B's explicit acceptance of passive capital as unproblematic.

items.stem: Which one of the following situations is most analogous to the change in the law that MacPherson effected, as that change is described in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A city stops requiring restaurants to pass periodic inspections and relies instead on complaints from customers to identify unsafe kitchens.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A lending library that had lent books only to residents of its own town begins lending to anyone and, at the same time, drops its rule that books be returned within two weeks.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A hospital that had treated only patients enrolled in its own health plan begins treating any patient, but only on condition that the patient pay the full charge in advance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A journal that had considered submissions only from members of its own faculty begins considering submissions from anyone and no longer sends them out for peer review.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A university that had admitted only the children of its graduates begins admitting any applicant, while continuing to require that every applicant meet the same academic standards it has always applied.

items.explanation: MacPherson changed who could sue without changing what a plaintiff had to prove: duty stopped depending on the contractual relationship and started depending on foreseeable use, but negligence still had to be shown. E has both halves — the relationship requirement drops, the substantive test stays. A abolishes the substantive test rather than the relationship. B and D drop both, which is precisely what the passage says Cardozo did not do. C opens the class of claimants but adds a new requirement, where MacPherson added none.

items.stem: In using the phrase "laundering old inequities through the authority of a number" (third paragraph), the author most likely means to convey that

choices.label: A
choices.text: the developers of risk-assessment instruments deliberately conceal the role that race plays in their formulas

choices.label: B
choices.text: a score can lend the appearance of an objective judgment about an individual to factors that in fact reflect pre-existing social disadvantage

choices.label: C
choices.text: numerical risk scores predict rearrest less accurately than the intuitive judgments of experienced judges do

choices.label: D
choices.text: courts have adopted risk-assessment instruments faster than they have subjected them to independent validation

choices.label: E
choices.text: the proprietary status of most instruments prevents a defendant from contesting the score he is assigned

items.explanation: The sentence describes a score that 'may in fact encode the circumstances of the neighborhood he was born into' while appearing to 'describe an individual's dangerousness' — disadvantage entering as though it were an objective finding about the person. B says that. A reads deliberate concealment into a paragraph that attributes the proxies to a scarcity of direct predictors. C compares accuracy, which this paragraph does not; the author's complaint is about what is measured. D belongs to the fourth paragraph's point about pace of adoption. E restates the transparency objection made two sentences earlier, not the metaphor asked about.

items.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tree-ring chronologies in Europe and the American Southwest now extend more than eight thousand years into the past.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The divergence problem shows that ring widths cannot be used to reconstruct past temperature.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tree rings can record climate quantitatively, but the conditions that make them do so also limit what a reconstruction can claim, so uncertainty and independent proxies are essential to the method.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Climate reconstruction should rely on ice cores and corals rather than on tree rings, whose weaknesses are now well documented.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trees growing at the margins of their range are more useful to climate science than trees growing in favourable conditions.

items.explanation: The passage builds a case and then qualifies it: rings carry a real climate signal (paragraph two), the very principle behind that signal creates the difficulties (paragraph three), and the response is to report uncertainty and cross-check other proxies (paragraph four). C carries all three movements. A and E are details from the first and third paragraphs. B overstates the divergence problem, which the passage treats as a limit rather than a refutation. D recommends abandoning tree rings, which the last paragraph explicitly refuses.

items.stem: According to the passage, a chronology can be extended beyond the lifetime of any single tree because

choices.label: A
choices.text: trees at the margins of a species' range live longer than trees in favourable conditions

choices.label: B
choices.text: the sequence of wide and narrow rings in a region is distinctive enough to match samples that overlap in time

choices.label: C
choices.text: a transfer function can be fitted wherever a chronology overlaps the instrumental record

choices.label: D
choices.text: ice cores and corals supply dates for the portions of a chronology that wood cannot cover

choices.label: E
choices.text: the factor limiting a tree's growth stays constant over the life of a stand

items.explanation: The first paragraph gives the reason directly: the pattern is a 'signature' of a particular run of years, so a pattern in living wood can be matched to the outer rings of older timber, and so on backward — B. C describes how a chronology is calibrated to climate, not how it is lengthened. D misuses the other proxies, which paragraph four offers as independent checks rather than as sources of dates. A is never claimed. E is contradicted by paragraph three, which turns on the limiting factor changing.

items.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the function of the third paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It supplies the historical background needed to understand the technique introduced in the first paragraph.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It presents evidence that the transfer functions described in the second paragraph have been fitted incorrectly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It shows that the feature of tree growth that makes the technique work is also the source of its principal difficulties.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It concedes an objection to the technique before dismissing the objection as unfounded.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It compares tree-ring chronologies with the independent proxies discussed in the final paragraph.

items.explanation: The paragraph opens by saying so: 'The method's difficulties follow from the same principle that gives it power,' and then works that out through the divergence problem and site selection — C. B misstates the divergence problem, which concerns a relationship that changed rather than arithmetic done wrongly. D has the paragraph dismissing the difficulties, which the passage never does. A offers background the paragraph does not contain, and E describes the comparison the fourth paragraph makes.

items.stem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following statements about site selection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sites chosen for the strength of their climate signal may for that very reason be unrepresentative of the surrounding landscape.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sites at the arid margin of a species' range yield more reliable chronologies than sites at treeline.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A site whose limiting factor has changed since 1960 should be excluded from a reconstruction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The longest chronologies have been assembled at sites where growth is limited by temperature rather than by moisture.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Researchers select stressed sites primarily because timber from such sites survives longer in old buildings.

items.explanation: The last sentence of paragraph three makes exactly this point: the stands with the cleanest signal are the marginal ones, and what limits growth at the margin need not limit it more widely — A. B ranks the two kinds of marginal site, which the passage never does; it describes both as signal-bearing. C prescribes an exclusion rule the passage does not offer, and its remedy is reported uncertainty and independent proxies. D connects chronology length to limiting factor, a link the passage never draws. E invents a reason for site selection in place of the one the passage gives.

items.stem: The author would be most likely to regard which one of the following reconstructions as meeting the standard set out in the final paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A reconstruction of regional rainfall from a single treeline chronology, presented as a single line and described as provisional in its introduction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A reconstruction of summer temperature that reports a confidence envelope widening with age and is compared against an ice-core record covering the same centuries.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A reconstruction that discards all post-1960 ring data on the ground that the divergence problem makes it unreliable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A reconstruction built from trees growing in unstressed conditions, so that no single factor dominates the growth signal.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A reconstruction that averages several tree-ring chronologies from one region and reports the mean without an estimate of error.

items.explanation: The paragraph asks for two things — an uncertainty envelope that widens as the calibration recedes, and a check against proxies whose weaknesses differ — and B is the only option with both, which is why it is correct. A calls itself provisional but still publishes the bare line the author says claims too much, and takes its signal from a single chronology. E fails the same test and its several chronologies are not independent in the required sense: they share a region and a proxy. C answers the divergence problem by deleting data rather than by reporting uncertainty. D removes the very stress that produces a readable signal, which paragraph three identifies as the reason marginal sites are chosen.

items.stem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of Passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Translations of poetry are less faithful than translations of statutes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pope's Homer is a better poem than any literal translation of Homer.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because a translation is a report about a text the reader cannot read, it should be faithful to what the original says rather than to the effect it produces.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The effect a poem produces is the same for every reader who encounters it in the original language.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A translator should not attempt to render poetry at all, since its words are part of what the reader is meant to experience.

items.explanation: Passage A states its thesis in the first paragraph — 'I take the opposite view' — and defends it in the second: a translation reports, and a report that changes what was said to reproduce a feeling is not one. C. D reverses A's argument, which turns on readers differing. B misreads the Pope example, granted as a fine poem and denied as a translation. A compares statutes and poems only to introduce the problem, and E recommends an abstention Passage A never counsels.

items.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passage B rejects a premise that Passage A's argument depends on and then limits its own position with a further constraint.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage B provides historical evidence for a claim that Passage A advances without support.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passage B applies Passage A's principle to a case Passage A does not consider.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage B and Passage A reach the same conclusion by different routes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage B concedes Passage A's central claim and disputes only its application to verse.

items.explanation: Passage B opens on the assumption behind A — that what a poem says can be separated from how it says it — and calls it 'close to false' in verse; its second paragraph then constrains its own view with the answerability test. That is A. E is the near miss: B does not concede A's central claim, it denies the separation the claim rests on. B and C describe cooperative moves the second passage never makes, and D is wrong because the two reach opposed conclusions.

items.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that the author of Passage B would regard a translation that renders every word by its dictionary sense and preserves nothing of the original's rhythm as

choices.label: A
choices.text: faithful in the only sense in which fidelity can be demanded

choices.label: B
choices.text: a summary of the original rather than a preservation of its meaning

choices.label: C
choices.text: an original poem occasioned by the source text

choices.label: D
choices.text: acceptable in prose but impossible to produce in verse

choices.label: E
choices.text: answerable to the original in the way Passage B's test requires

items.explanation: Passage B says it in terms: such a rendering 'has not preserved the meaning while sacrificing the form, it has preserved a summary' — B. A states the literalist position B is arguing against. C borrows Passage A's description of effect-chasing translation, which is the opposite failing. D contradicts B, whose complaint is that the thing is entirely possible and inadequate. E inverts the answerability test, which licenses departures that carry over an effect the source has.

items.stem: Both passages are committed to which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A translator's departures from the literal sense of the original require justification.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The effect a poem produces varies from reader to reader.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Verse and prose place the same demands on a translator.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A translation that reads well as a poem in its own language has probably departed too far from its original.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The meaning of a line of verse includes the expectation set up by its rhyme.

items.explanation: Passage A holds that altering what was said is not reporting at all; Passage B allows departures but only where each one is 'answerable to something in the original'. Both therefore treat a departure as needing a warrant, which is A — they disagree about what can supply it. B is Passage A's premise and no part of B's argument. E is Passage B's claim about meaning, which Passage A denies. C is denied by both, each of which distinguishes verse from prose or statute. D is asserted by neither: Passage A calls Pope's Homer a fine thing and objects only to calling it a translation.

items.stem: Suppose a translator renders a source poem's short, hammering line as a longer English line, on the ground that the English line's stresses fall where the original's do. The author of Passage A and the author of Passage B would be most likely to disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the translator has produced a poem worth reading in English

choices.label: B
choices.text: the stresses of the original fall where the translator says they do

choices.label: C
choices.text: carrying over the original's stress pattern can justify departing from its literal sense

choices.label: D
choices.text: translating verse is more difficult than translating prose

choices.label: E
choices.text: the translator should have consulted a bilingual dictionary

items.explanation: The example is designed to isolate one question: an effect of the original has been carried over at the cost of the words. Passage B's answerability test licenses exactly that; Passage A holds that a rendering which alters what was said to reproduce how it felt is not a report — so C is the point of disagreement. A is a judgement Passage A would grant a good effect-driven translation, as it grants Pope. B is a factual question about the source neither author addresses. D is common ground: both distinguish verse from other kinds of text. E concerns method rather than the standard by which a rendering is judged.

items.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: MacPherson v. Buick Motor Co. relieved injured plaintiffs of the burden of proving that a manufacturer had been negligent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nineteenth-century courts defended the privity requirement as protection for a young industrial economy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Section 402A of the Restatement (Second) of Torts codified strict liability for defective products in 1965.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Justice Traynor's concurrence in Escola was the single most important opinion in the development of products-liability law.

choices.label: E
choices.text: American products-liability law moved from a privity bar through negligence to strict liability, but negligence reasoning survives within the modern regime.

items.explanation: The passage traces three stages and then argues in its last paragraph that the third is less clean a break than its label suggests — E. A misstates MacPherson, which the second paragraph says left the negligence requirement standing. B and C are true details from the first and third paragraphs, not the point they serve. D ranks Escola against every other opinion, a comparison the passage never makes.

items.stem: Which one of the following, if it occurred, would best illustrate the passage's claim that strict liability's label "can obscure how much negligence reasoning survives within it"?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A court deciding a design-defect claim asks whether the danger the design created was justified by what the design achieved, and rules for the manufacturer because it was.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A court holds a bottler liable for a bottle that shattered in a customer's hand without inquiring what care the bottler took.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A court dismisses a claim because the injured plaintiff bought the product from a retailer rather than from the manufacturer.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A court allows a bystander injured by a defective machine to sue the manufacturer although he never bought or used it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A legislature requires manufacturers to carry insurance so that the cost of product injuries is spread across all purchasers.

items.explanation: The claim is that a doctrine labelled strict still runs on the risk-versus-utility balancing that negligence performs. A is that balancing, done under a strict-liability heading — the passage names design-defect cases as where it happens. B is strict liability working as advertised, with fault dropped rather than smuggled in. C applies the privity rule the passage says fell, and D is MacPherson's foreseeability principle. E enacts the risk-distribution rationale, which the passage distinguishes from negligence reasoning rather than identifying with it.

items.stem: According to the passage, ring width at a site near the cold upper limit of a species' range varies chiefly with

choices.label: A
choices.text: the precipitation the site receives

choices.label: B
choices.text: the age of the oldest tree in the stand

choices.label: C
choices.text: the number of overlapping samples available for cross-dating

choices.label: D
choices.text: summer temperature

choices.label: E
choices.text: the width of the rings recorded at nearby arid sites

items.explanation: The second paragraph divides the two kinds of marginal site: at the arid lower limit growth is limited by water, and at the cold upper limit near treeline it is limited by warmth, so ring width there varies with summer temperature — D. A gives the answer for the other kind of site. B, C and E name things the passage discusses — stand age, cross-dating, other chronologies — but never connects to what a treeline ring's width tracks.

items.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the author's attitude toward actuarial risk-assessment instruments?

choices.label: A
choices.text: unqualified opposition, grounded in the instruments' reliance on proxies that track race

choices.label: B
choices.text: enthusiasm tempered only by concern that some instruments are proprietary

choices.label: C
choices.text: acceptance in principle, joined to the objection that the safeguards their use requires have not kept pace with their adoption

choices.label: D
choices.text: indifference as to whether the instruments displace judicial discretion, so long as disparities are documented

choices.label: E
choices.text: confidence that independent validation has already answered the criticisms the instruments have attracted

items.explanation: The fourth paragraph states the position outright: the instruments are not worthless, they might yet deliver what was promised if validated and stripped of the worst proxies, and the reservation is 'narrower but firm' — adoption has outrun the safeguards. C. A is the answer for a writer who condemned them wholesale, which this author explicitly declines to do. B reduces the objection to proprietary status and misses the proxies. D attributes an indifference the second paragraph contradicts. E reverses the complaint: validation is what the author says is missing.

items.stem: Which one of the following is a claim made in Passage B that the author of Passage A would be most likely to reject?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Translating verse makes demands that translating prose does not.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A translator's departures from the literal sense require justification.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A translation that reproduces the effect of its original may be a fine poem.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some renderings are better understood as original poems occasioned by their sources.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A rendering that keeps the dictionary sense of every word while discarding the original's movement has not preserved its meaning.

items.explanation: Passage A's whole case rests on meaning being what a report carries over, so a faithful-to-sense rendering preserves it; Passage B's claim in E denies exactly that, calling such a rendering a summary. The two cannot both hold, which is why E is the point of rejection. A is common ground — Passage A opens by distinguishing verse from statute. B is shared as well: A allows no departures without warrant and B demands answerability. C and D are Passage A's own claims about Pope, not Passage B's.
